title: Four Lenses With Which to Observe Lessons
author: Nick Hart
summary: Setting aside the reliability problems of grading lessons, Hart offers school leaders four lenses for what to look at when they observe, arranged from downstream to upstream. The first is understanding in the lesson, judged by children's responses rather than the teacher's performance, because an observer's own prior knowledge makes explanations look clearer than pupils experienced them - and learning itself cannot be seen in an hour. The second places the lesson in its sequence, looking back through books and forward to the unit's end point and key-stage outcomes. The third turns the observation back on leadership: how did CPD, collaboration and advocated strategies produce this teacher's decisions, whether the lesson went well or badly? The fourth is what co-observers notice, which he treats as a culture-setting moment that determines what a school talks about. He argues that the senior observer, in particular, should not watch a lesson in isolation, and that paired observation with deliberate discussion beats solo judgement.
points: Hart separates what is visible in a lesson - engagement, emotion, understanding - from learning, which happens over time and cannot be seen in one observation.
Because observers bring expert prior knowledge, he argues their judgement should be weighted toward children's reactions, talk and work rather than the teacher's explanations.
He proposes a division of labour in paired observations: the less senior colleague, closer to the classroom, watches understanding while the senior leader uses the wider lenses.
Lens 3 makes observation an audit of leadership itself, asking what CPD and planning support produced this lesson and whether teachers' collaboration time is being wasted.
The post-observation discussion among observers sets culture by revealing what leaders notice, which is why he warns against feedback that fixates on displays, book presentation or typos.
quotes: Learning doesn’t happen in neat, one hour blocks. When we’re observing lessons, we of course need to be attuned to the ultimate outcome of impact on children’s learning but we shouldn’t fool ourselves into thinking we can see it in a lesson.

However clear and well designed we think explanations and tasks were, the children may not have experienced them in the same way because they won’t have the prior knowledge that we possess. So we have to weight an opinion more heavily on children’s responses to what the teacher has done. Watch their reactions.

I think it is a mistake to observe a lesson in isolation, particularly if you are a senior leader. Subject leaders and senior leaders ought to think wider. What do we know about outcomes years down the line?
If the teacher has run into difficulties, I want to think about the missed opportunities. How did this lesson come about? What did the team talk about in their planing meeting?
Equally, I want to explore attribution. Has this teacher thrived without engaging in any planned collaboration? Are we wasting teachers’ time at all?

Headteachers and Principals, I’d argue, should be more concerned with systems thinking and capacity building, even when observing lessons. Observing with a colleague is infinitely more valuable than observing alone because of the opportunities to discuss what you’ve noticed and reflect on biases.

But talking about Y could result in some valuable emergence of joint understanding and practice development that may not have happened if we stick solely to the agreed areas of focus. This ultimately comes down to trust and the perceived attitudes of observers in the minds of those being observed.
